# What You Will Learn in Unit 4

In Units 1-3 you learned *what* AI is, *how* to explore data, and *how* to evaluate models. **Unit 4 is where you finally build the models** — and you point them at the things civil engineers care about: concrete, pipes, pavements, floods, crops, heat, landslides, and rivers. Then you connect ML to **maps**, because almost every civil engineering decision has a *location*.

By the end of this handout, you will be able to:

1. **Fit and interpret regression models** — linear for continuous targets (concrete strength), logistic for binary outcomes (pipe failure). _(CO4)_
2. **Build tree-based models** — decision trees and random forests — and read their variable-importance and partial-dependence plots. _(CO4, CO5)_
3. **Apply proximity and probability classifiers** — KNN and Naive Bayes — and know when each is appropriate. _(CO4)_
4. **Cluster unlabeled data** — K-means and hierarchical — to create homogeneous zones for planning. _(CO4)_
5. **Work with geospatial data** — rasters vs. vectors in R with `terra` and `sf`. _(CO6)_
6. **Process satellite imagery** — build NDVI maps and vegetation masks. _(CO6)_
7. **Fuse GIS with AI** — the `extract()` → model → `predict()` workflow that powers every modern susceptibility map. _(CO6)_
8. **Deliver advanced mapping products** — Urban Heat Island maps, landslide susceptibility zones, and river change detection. _(CO6)_

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil connection:** Every algorithm in this unit is illustrated with a civil engineering dataset — concrete mixes, water pipelines, pavements, flood sites, crop yields, cities, slopes, and rivers. The tools are general; the problems are the ones you will meet on site.
:::

::: {.tipbox}
**How to use this handout:** Read a section, then run its code chunk in RStudio (or knit the whole file). Every dataset is **simulated inside the document**, so everything knits reproducibly on any laptop — even offline. At the end of each section we tell you where real datasets live (Bhuvan, USGS, Copernicus, Kaggle) so you can swap in real data during project work.
:::

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the outputs:** Wherever a code chunk prints a table or a figure, the section immediately after it (marked with a purple bar like this one) explains what you are looking at, what it means, and what to watch out for.
:::

# Regression Models

## Linear Regression for Structural Design

### The idea in one line

Fit the straight line $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ that minimizes the sum of squared vertical errors:

$$\min_{\beta_0,\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\right)^2$$

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** You have done this physically already. When you draw the **initial tangent modulus** on a stress–strain curve, or a best-fit line through **load–deflection** readings of a beam test, you are fitting a linear regression by eye. The slope $\beta_1$ is a *stiffness-like* quantity; the residuals are your *measurement scatter*.
:::

### Simulate a concrete mix dataset

Physical truth we encode: **strength decreases as water–cement ratio increases** (Abrams' law), improves with cement content, and grows with age.

```{r lin-sim}
n <- 150
concrete <- tibble(
  mix_id = sprintf("M%03d", 1:n),
  wc     = round(runif(n, 0.38, 0.72), 3), # water-cement ratio
  cement = round(runif(n, 300, 500), 0), # kg/m3
  age    = sample(c(7, 28, 90), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2))
)

age_fac <- case_when(
  concrete$age == 7 ~ 0.78,
  concrete$age == 28 ~ 1.00,
  concrete$age == 90 ~ 1.12
)

set.seed(11)
concrete <- concrete %>%
  mutate(strength = round(65 * age_fac * (cement / 400)^0.4 *
    exp(-1.8 * (wc - 0.45)) + rnorm(n, 0, 2.5), 1))

head(concrete)
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** Each row is one concrete mix. `wc`, `cement`, and `age` are inputs; `strength` is the target. The last column is what we will try to predict. The simulation encodes Abrams' law (higher `wc` → lower strength), a mild cement effect, and age-dependence through `age_fac`.
:::

### Fit and visualize

```{r lin-fit-fig, fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Linear regression: strength falls as w/c rises — Abrams' law recovered from data."}
fit1 <- lm(strength ~ wc, data = concrete)
b0 <- coef(fit1)[1]
b1 <- coef(fit1)[2]
r2 <- summary(fit1)$r.squared

ggplot(concrete, aes(wc, strength)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.65, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "firebrick", fill = "pink") +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.71, y = max(concrete$strength) - 1,
    label = sprintf("strength = %.1f %+.1f × w/c\nR² = %.2f", b0, b1, r2),
    hjust = 1, size = 4.2, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Simple linear regression: concrete strength vs w/c ratio",
    x = "Water-cement ratio (w/c)",
    y = "Compressive strength (MPa)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** Each blue dot is one mix. The red line is the fitted regression; the pink band is its 95% confidence interval. The annotation shows the equation and R². **Reading the coefficients:** $\beta_1 \approx -60$ MPa per unit w/c. Because w/c moves in steps of 0.1, each 0.1 increase in w/c costs roughly **6 MPa** — exactly the rule of thumb used in mix-design labs. R² near 0.6–0.7 would be typical here: w/c alone explains most, but not all, of the strength variation.
:::

### Always check residuals (Unit 3 pays off!)

```{r lin-diag, fig.width=9, fig.height=6.5, fig.cap="The four classic diagnostic plots from Unit 3, now applied to a structural model."}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit1, pch = 19, col = "steelblue", cex = 0.7)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**What to look for:**

- *Residuals vs Fitted* — should look like a random cloud (no funnel, no curve). A curve here means the relationship is not really linear.
- *Normal Q-Q* — points should hug the diagonal. Strong departures mean the errors are not normal, which weakens confidence intervals.
- *Scale-Location* — no growing spread (heteroscedasticity). A funnel shape means the model is less reliable at high strengths.
- *Residuals vs Leverage* — watch for influential mixes (bad lab data). Points in the top-right corner can single-handedly tilt the whole line.
:::

### Multiple regression: add cement content and age

```{r lin-multi}
fit2 <- lm(strength ~ wc + cement + factor(age), data = concrete)
summary(fit2)$r.squared
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this output:** The single number printed is the **multiple R²** — the fraction of strength variance explained by *all three* predictors together. You should see it climb noticeably above the simple-regression R². That jump is the payoff of adding features that carry real physical information: cement content and curing age both matter, and the model uses them.
:::

```{r lin-obsfit, fig.width=6.8, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Observed vs fitted strength, coloured by curing age — points hug the 1:1 line."}
concrete$fitted2 <- fitted(fit2)
ggplot(concrete, aes(fitted2, strength, colour = factor(age))) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Age (days)") +
  labs(
    title = "Multiple regression fits better than simple regression",
    x = "Predicted strength (MPa)", y = "Observed strength (MPa)"
  ) +
  coord_equal()
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The dashed diagonal is the perfect-prediction line `y = x`. A good model puts points tightly around it. Compare the scatter here to what you would see from the simple model — the tighter and more symmetric the cloud, the better the fit. Colours let you check whether the model is systematically wrong for a particular age group (e.g., always under-predicting 7-day cubes).
:::

### Predict a new mix (with uncertainty)

```{r lin-predict}
new_mix <- data.frame(
  wc = 0.45, cement = 420,
  age = factor(28, levels = sort(unique(concrete$age)))
)
predict(fit2, new_mix, interval = "predict")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this output:** The `fit` column is the point prediction of 28-day strength for a mix with w/c = 0.45 and 420 kg/m³ of cement. The `lwr`–`upr` pair is the **prediction interval** — the range in which a *single future cube* from this mix will fall with 95% probability. It is much wider than a confidence interval for the mean, because batch-to-batch variability is included. This is the number a careful engineer quotes to the client.
:::

::: {.civilbox}
**Where linear regression appears in CE practice:** concrete strength, settlement vs. log-time, beam deflection vs. span⁴ (linear in the coefficients), trip generation vs. floor area, flood discharge vs. catchment area (rating curves).
:::

## Logistic Regression for Failure Prediction

### The idea in one line

We want a **probability** of failure, not a number. Logistic regression passes the familiar linear score through an S-curve:

$$p = P(y=1) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad z = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 + \dots$$

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** A *factor of safety* does not tell you "the structure fails or not" — it tells you how *close* you are. The sigmoid is the statistical factor-of-safety: it converts a linear "danger score" into a probability between 0 and 1.
:::

```{r log-sigmoid, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="The sigmoid squashes any real number into a probability. The dashed line is the 0.5 decision threshold."}
z <- seq(-8, 8, length.out = 400)
tibble(z = z, p = plogis(z)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(z, p)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.4, y = 0.56, label = "decision threshold\np = 0.5", size = 3.4, colour = "grey30") +
  annotate("text", x = -4.6, y = 0.18, label = "z very negative\n→ 'asset healthy'", size = 3.4, colour = "steelblue") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.6, y = 0.82, label = "z very positive\n→ 'asset failing'", size = 3.4, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)) +
  labs(
    x = "z = β0 + β1·age + β2·pressure  (linear danger score)",
    y = "P(failure)", title = "The sigmoid function"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The horizontal axis is the linear score $z$ (however big or small the "danger" signal is). The vertical axis is the resulting **probability**. Notice that no matter how extreme $z$ is, the output is always between 0 and 1 — that is what a probability must do. The dashed line at 0.5 is only a *default* cutoff; Section 3 will show you how to move it.
:::

### Simulate a water-pipeline failure dataset

```{r log-sim}
set.seed(21)
n_pipe <- 400
pipe <- tibble(
  age      = round(runif(n_pipe, 1, 40), 1), # years in service
  pressure = round(runif(n_pipe, 1, 6), 2) # average operating pressure (bar)
) %>%
  mutate(
    logit   = -6 + 0.08 * age + 0.55 * pressure,
    prob    = plogis(logit),
    failure = rbinom(n_pipe, 1, prob) # 1 = burst/leak recorded
  )
mean(pipe$failure)
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** The last printed number is the **base rate** of failure in the dataset. It should be well below 0.5 — pipe failures are rare events. That matters because it drives which metric you trust later (Unit 3 lesson: recall over accuracy for rare events).
:::

### Fit the model and interpret coefficients

```{r log-fit}
fit_logit <- glm(failure ~ age + pressure, data = pipe, family = binomial)

tibble(
  term       = names(coef(fit_logit)),
  beta       = round(coef(fit_logit), 4),
  odds_ratio = round(exp(coef(fit_logit)), 3)
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read an odds ratio:** $e^{\beta}$. For age, $e^{0.08} \approx 1.08$: every extra service year **multiplies the odds of failure by 1.08** (≈ 8% growth per year, compounding). This is exactly how maintenance engineers talk about *deterioration rates*. For pressure, $e^{0.55} \approx 1.73$: each extra bar of operating pressure multiplies failure odds by ~1.73 — a very strong effect, as pipe engineers expect.
:::

### The decision boundary on the age–pressure plane

```{r log-boundary, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="Background colour = model-predicted failure probability. The white region is 'safe operating envelope'."}
grid <- expand.grid(
  age = seq(0, 40, length.out = 160),
  pressure = seq(1, 6, length.out = 160)
)
grid$prob <- predict(fit_logit, newdata = grid, type = "response")

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid, aes(age, pressure, fill = prob)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "P(failure)") +
  geom_point(
    data = pipe, aes(age, pressure, colour = factor(failure)),
    size = 1.6, alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("0" = "grey20", "1" = "red"),
    labels = c("No failure", "Failure"), name = "Observed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Pipeline failure model: probability landscape",
    x = "Pipe age (years)", y = "Operating pressure (bar)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The background colour is the model's *predicted* probability of failure at every (age, pressure) combination. Dark purple = safe; yellow = dangerous. Overlaid points are the real observed outcomes — black = no failure, red = failure. A good model puts red dots in yellow regions and black dots in purple regions. The **white diagonal** is the 0.5 contour — a practical safe-operating envelope. Anything above-right of it needs maintenance priority.
:::

### Evaluation: confusion matrix, threshold tuning, ROC

```{r log-conf, fig.width=6, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Confusion matrix at the default 0.5 threshold."}
prob_pred <- predict(fit_logit, type = "response")
pred_class <- ifelse(prob_pred > 0.5, 1, 0)
cm <- table(Predicted = pred_class, Actual = pipe$failure)

as.data.frame(cm) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Actual, Predicted, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 7, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "Confusion matrix — pipeline failures")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the confusion matrix:** Each cell counts cases. The top-left cell is True Negative (we said "no failure", and there was none). The bottom-right is True Positive (we predicted failure, it failed — good catch). The bottom-left is False Negative — a **missed failure**, which in a water utility means an unplanned burst. The top-right is a False Positive — a maintenance truck sent out for nothing.
:::

```{r log-threshold, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Moving the threshold trades precision against recall — the water board chooses based on repair budget."}
metrics <- purrr::map_dfr(seq(0.05, 0.95, 0.01), function(t) {
  pred <- as.integer(prob_pred > t)
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & pipe$failure == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & pipe$failure == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & pipe$failure == 1)
  tibble(
    threshold = t,
    accuracy = mean(pred == pipe$failure),
    precision = tp / max(tp + fp, 1),
    recall = tp / max(tp + fn, 1)
  )
})

metrics %>%
  pivot_longer(-threshold) %>%
  ggplot(aes(threshold, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(
    title = "Threshold tuning: no single threshold wins everything",
    x = "Probability threshold", y = "Metric value", colour = NULL
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** As the threshold moves left (more warnings), **recall rises** (we catch more real failures) but **precision falls** (more false alarms). As it moves right, the reverse. Accuracy is a misleading flat curve — for rare events it barely moves, because most cases are non-failures regardless. The engineering decision is which trade-off you can afford: a utility with a large repair crew can tolerate low precision; one with a small crew cannot.
:::

```{r log-roc, fig.width=6, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="ROC curve for the pipeline failure model."}
roc_fit <- roc(pipe$failure, prob_pred, quiet = TRUE)
roc_df <- tibble(
  fpr = 1 - roc_fit$specificities,
  tpr = roc_fit$sensitivities
) %>% arrange(fpr, tpr)

ggplot(roc_df, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_path(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0.62, y = 0.12, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold",
    label = sprintf("AUC = %.3f", auc(roc_fit))
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "ROC — logistic failure model",
    x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the ROC curve:** The horizontal axis is the false-alarm rate; the vertical is the true-positive rate. The dashed diagonal is a useless model. The red curve bulges upward — the closer to the top-left corner, the better. AUC of ~0.85 is a strong utility-grade classifier; the printed value in your run will land in that range.
:::

::: {.civilbox}
**Real CE uses of logistic regression:** pipe burst prediction (water utilities worldwide), pavement failure within analysis period, slope failure yes/no, contractor bid win/loss, defect presence in bridge inspection records.
:::

---

# Tree-Based Models

## Decision Trees

### The idea in one line

Repeatedly split the data with yes/no questions, choosing the split that makes groups **purer**. Purity is measured by **Gini impurity** $G = 1-\sum_k p_k^2$ or **entropy** $H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k$.

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** A decision tree is literally the **maintenance flowchart** in your inspection manual: *"Is IRI > 4.5? → Is rutting > 10 mm? → Overlay vs. Reconstruction."* ML discovers the flowchart from data instead of from committee meetings.
:::

### Simulate a pavement-management dataset

```{r tree-sim}
set.seed(31)
n_sec <- 400
pavement <- tibble(
  section = sprintf("S%04d", 1:n_sec),
  age     = round(runif(n_sec, 1, 25), 1), # years since construction
  traffic = round(runif(n_sec, 0.2, 12), 2), # million ESALs / year
  rut     = round(runif(n_sec, 2, 14), 1) # mm rut depth
) %>%
  mutate(
    IRI = 0.8 + 0.055 * age + 0.18 * traffic + 0.08 * rut + rnorm(n_sec, 0, 0.45),
    condition = cut(IRI,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 2.7, 4.2, Inf),
      labels = c("Good", "Fair", "Poor")
    )
  )
table(pavement$condition)
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** The table shows how many pavement sections fall into each condition class (Good, Fair, Poor). The classes are ordered by IRI thresholds used in highway practice. A well-balanced dataset has all three classes represented; if one class dominates, we would worry about class imbalance later.
:::

### Train / test split and tree fitting

```{r tree-train}
set.seed(7)
idx <- sample(seq_len(n_sec), size = 0.7 * n_sec)
train_p <- pavement[idx, ]
test_p <- pavement[-idx, ]

tree_pav <- rpart(condition ~ age + traffic + rut,
  data = train_p,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(minsplit = 20, cp = 0.01)
)
```

```{r tree-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, fig.cap="The learned decision tree. Each box shows the majority class and class probabilities."}
rpart.plot(tree_pav,
  type = 4, extra = 104, box.palette = "auto",
  shadow.col = "grey", cex = 0.85
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the tree diagram:** Start at the top node — the tree has chosen the single most informative question to ask first. Follow the yes/no branches downward. Each **leaf** (bottom box) shows the majority class and the class probabilities. Here the tree typically asks about `traffic` or `age` first — rediscovering that heavy, old pavements deteriorate first. Colour depth indicates the predicted class.
:::

### How a tree carves up feature space

```{r tree-partition, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Decision trees create rectangular regions — axis-aligned cuts, one at a time."}
tree_2d <- rpart(condition ~ age + traffic,
  data = train_p, method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01)
)
grid_p <- expand.grid(
  age = seq(1, 25, length.out = 200),
  traffic = seq(0.2, 12, length.out = 200)
)
grid_p$pred <- predict(tree_2d, grid_p, type = "class")

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = grid_p, aes(age, traffic, fill = pred), alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_point(data = train_p, aes(age, traffic, colour = condition), size = 1.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(Good = "palegreen3", Fair = "khaki1", Poor = "indianred1"),
    name = "Predicted"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(Good = "darkgreen", Fair = "darkgoldenrod3", Poor = "firebrick"),
    name = "Actual"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Tree partitions of the age × traffic plane",
    x = "Pavement age (years)", y = "Traffic (M ESALs/yr)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The background colour shows what the tree *predicts* at each (age, traffic) coordinate. The dots are the actual data. Notice the **rectangular, axis-aligned boundaries** — a tree splits one feature at a time. That is both a strength (easy to interpret) and a weakness (boundaries look blocky compared to reality).
:::

### Pruning: choosing tree size with the complexity parameter

```{r tree-cp, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.cap="plotcp(): pick the smallest tree within one SE of the minimum — the same overfitting story as Unit 3."}
plotcp(tree_pav)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this plot:** The horizontal axis is the complexity parameter `cp` (larger cp = simpler tree). The vertical axis is cross-validated error. The dashed horizontal line is one standard error above the minimum. **The rule:** pick the simplest tree whose error is still within that band — this avoids overfitting while keeping the model small enough to explain to a maintenance crew.
:::

### Test performance

```{r tree-conf}
pred_tree <- predict(tree_pav, newdata = test_p, type = "class")
cm_tree <- table(Predicted = pred_tree, Actual = test_p$condition)
cm_tree
sprintf("Test accuracy = %.1f%%", 100 * sum(diag(cm_tree)) / sum(cm_tree))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the confusion matrix:** Rows are what the tree predicted, columns are what actually happened. The diagonal cells (top-left, middle, bottom-right) are correct classifications. Off-diagonal cells are mistakes — for a pavement manager, a "Poor predicted as Good" mistake is the most dangerous (it leads to no intervention on a road that needs one).
:::

## Random Forests

### The idea in one line

Train many decorrelated trees on **bootstrap samples** with **random feature subsets**, then vote (classification) or average (regression). The wisdom of the crowd beats any single expert.

$$\hat{y} = \text{majority}\big\{T_1(x), T_2(x), \dots, T_B(x)\big\}$$

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** One inspector can be biased; a **panel of five independent inspectors** averaging their condition ratings is far more reliable. Random forest = a panel of 500 slightly-different decision trees. Bonus: each tree never saw ~37% of the data (**out-of-bag**, OOB) — a free built-in test set, like each inspector skipping some buildings and cross-checking the others.
:::

```{r rf-concept, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Bagging: bootstrap samples → diverse trees → majority vote."}
rf_boxes <- tibble(
  x    = rep(c(2.5, 6.0, 9.5), each = 3),
  y    = c(3.0, 2.2, 3.0, 2.2, 3.0, 2.2, 3.0, 2.2, 3.0),
  lab  = "Tree",
  fill = "#4C72B0"
)
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 1, xmax = 4, ymin = 0.8, ymax = 4.2, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey60") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 4.5, label = "Bootstrap samples\n+ random features", size = 3.2) +
  geom_point(data = rf_boxes, aes(x, y), shape = 15, size = 9, colour = "#4C72B0") +
  annotate("text", x = 6.0, y = 2.6, label = "500\ntrees\nvote", size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 8.2, xmax = 10.8, ymin = 1.8, ymax = 3.4, fill = "#C44E52", colour = "grey20") +
  annotate("text", x = 9.5, y = 2.6, label = "Majority vote\n= prediction", colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("segment",
    x = 4.05, xend = 5.3, y = 2.6, yend = 2.6,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), linewidth = 1
  ) +
  annotate("segment",
    x = 6.7, xend = 8.15, y = 2.6, yend = 2.6,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm")), linewidth = 1
  ) +
  xlim(0.5, 11) +
  ylim(0.5, 5) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Random forest = bagged, decorrelated decision trees")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this schematic:** Each tree is trained on a different bootstrap sample (random rows with replacement) and only considers a random subset of features at each split. This "forced diversity" is what makes the trees disagree — and disagreement is what makes the crowd smarter than any one member. The final prediction is a majority vote (or, in regression, an average).
:::

### Simulate a flood susceptibility dataset

Flood susceptibility mapping uses **terrain + climate factors**: low elevation, gentle slope, high rainfall, close to river, sparse vegetation (low NDVI) → flood-prone.

```{r rf-flood-sim}
set.seed(41)
n_sites <- 600
flood_sites <- tibble(
  elevation  = round(runif(n_sites, 5, 200), 1), # metres
  slope      = round(runif(n_sites, 0.5, 25), 1), # percent
  rainfall   = round(runif(n_sites, 600, 1800), 0), # mm/year
  dist_river = round(runif(n_sites, 20, 1500), 0), # metres
  ndvi       = round(runif(n_sites, 0.05, 0.8), 2)
) %>%
  mutate(
    logit = 1.6 - 0.035 * elevation - 0.09 * slope + 0.0035 * rainfall -
      0.0022 * dist_river - 2.0 * ndvi,
    flood = factor(ifelse(rbinom(n_sites, 1, plogis(logit)) == 1, "yes", "no"),
      levels = c("no", "yes")
    )
  )
mean(flood_sites$flood == "yes") # prevalence of flood observations
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** The last number is the **base rate of flooding** in the simulated dataset. It typically falls in the 10–30% range — a moderately imbalanced problem. That is realistic for susceptibility studies: floods happen, but rarely at any given site.
:::

### Train the forest

```{r rf-train}
set.seed(42)
f_idx <- sample(seq_len(n_sites), 0.7 * n_sites)
flood_train <- flood_sites[f_idx, ]
flood_test <- flood_sites[-f_idx, ]

rf_flood <- randomForest(flood ~ elevation + slope + rainfall + dist_river + ndvi,
  data = flood_train, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE
)
rf_flood
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the printed forest:** The output prints the number of trees, the OOB (out-of-bag) confusion matrix, and the OOB error rate for each class. **The OOB error is a free validation estimate** — it was computed on data each tree never saw, so it is honest. If OOB error is ~0.1, the forest is achieving ~90% accuracy on held-out rows.
:::

### Watch the OOB error converge as trees are added

```{r rf-oob, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Out-of-bag error vs number of trees. After ~200 trees, adding more helps very little — that is the forest 'converging'."}
as.data.frame(rf_flood$err.rate) %>%
  mutate(tree = row_number()) %>%
  pivot_longer(-tree, names_to = "metric") %>%
  ggplot(aes(tree, value, colour = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Random forest learning curve (OOB error)",
    x = "Number of trees", y = "Error rate", colour = NULL
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** Each curve tracks the OOB error for one class (and the overall). Error drops steeply at first, then flattens. The **knee** (usually around 100–250 trees) is where adding more trees stops helping. Beyond that you are just burning CPU time. This is how practitioners decide `ntree`.
:::

### Which factors drive flooding? Variable importance

```{r rf-varimp, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Variable importance: rainfall and distance-to-river dominate — matches hydrological intuition."}
varImpPlot(rf_flood, main = "Flood susceptibility: which factors matter most?")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the variable importance plot:** Two panels are printed — one for mean decrease in accuracy, one for mean decrease in Gini. Higher = more important. **`rainfall` and `dist_river` typically dominate** — matches hydrological intuition (more rain + closer to a river = more flooding). `elevation` matters next; `ndvi` is usually weakest in this setup. If a factor you *know* matters shows up near the bottom, investigate — that is a signal your features or simulation may need rethinking.
:::

### Partial dependence: how does probability respond to one factor?

```{r rf-pdp, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Partial dependence: holding everything else constant, flood probability rises with rainfall and falls with elevation."}
pd_rain <- partial(rf_flood,
  pred.var = "rainfall",
  which.class = "yes", train = flood_train,
  prob = TRUE, plot = FALSE
)
pd_elev <- partial(rf_flood,
  pred.var = "elevation",
  which.class = "yes", train = flood_train,
  prob = TRUE, plot = FALSE
)

p1 <- ggplot(pd_rain, aes(rainfall, yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of rainfall",
    x = "Annual rainfall (mm)", y = "P(flood)"
  )

p2 <- ggplot(pd_elev, aes(elevation, yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of elevation",
    x = "Elevation (m)", y = "P(flood)"
  )

p1 | p2
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read partial dependence plots:** These show the model's *average* predicted probability as one feature sweeps across its range, holding everything else constant. **Steep curves = strong effect**; flat curves = the model does not use that feature much. A monotonic rise with rainfall and monotonic fall with elevation is physically sensible — a curved or non-monotonic shape would reveal a **threshold** the forest has discovered on its own.
:::

### Test-set ROC

```{r rf-roc, fig.width=6, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="ROC curve on the held-out flood sites."}
prob_rf <- predict(rf_flood, newdata = flood_test, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
roc_rf <- roc(flood_test$flood, prob_rf,
  levels = c("no", "yes"),
  direction = "<", quiet = TRUE
)
sprintf("Test AUC = %.3f", auc(roc_rf))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the AUC:** A number is printed — the area under the ROC on the held-out test sites. **AUC = 0.5** is guessing; **AUC = 0.9+** is excellent. Values above 0.85 are typical for well-featured flood susceptibility models. This is the honest number to quote in a report — not the OOB error, and never the training error.
:::

### Bonus application: crop yield (regression forest)

```{r rf-yield}
set.seed(51)
n_farm <- 350
farms <- tibble(
  rainfall   = round(runif(n_farm, 400, 1600), 0), # mm / season
  fertilizer = round(runif(n_farm, 40, 180), 0), # kg/ha
  soil_index = round(runif(n_farm, 1, 10), 1), # 1 (poor) to 10 (excellent)
  ndvi_peak  = round(runif(n_farm, 0.2, 0.85), 2)
) %>%
  mutate(yield = round(pmax(1.2 + 0.004 * rainfall + 0.012 * fertilizer +
    0.25 * soil_index + 2.2 * ndvi_peak +
    rnorm(n_farm, 0, 0.5), 0.5), 2))

rf_yield <- randomForest(yield ~ ., data = farms, ntree = 400, importance = TRUE)
sprintf("OOB R² = %.3f", tail(rf_yield$rsq, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** The last number is the **out-of-bag R²** for the yield regression. Above 0.7 = the model explains most yield variation. Random forests work for regression exactly as they do for classification: averaging individual tree predictions gives a smoother, more accurate result than any single tree.
:::

```{r rf-yield-figs, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Crop yield forest: variable importance (left) and OOB-predicted vs observed yield (right)."}
imp_df <- as_tibble(importance(rf_yield)[, "%IncMSE"], rownames = "variable")
colnames(imp_df) <- c("variable", "value")

p_imp <- ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(variable, value), y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Yield drivers (%IncMSE)", x = NULL, y = "% increase in MSE")

p_scatter <- tibble(observed = farms$yield, oob = rf_yield$predicted) %>%
  ggplot(aes(oob, observed)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "OOB predictions vs observations",
    x = "Predicted yield (t/ha)", y = "Observed yield (t/ha)"
  ) +
  coord_equal()

p_imp | p_scatter
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the two panels:**

- **Left:** Variable importance. Bars are the % increase in MSE that results when each variable is shuffled (larger = more important). The top bar is the yield driver the forest relies on most — typically `ndvi_peak` or `rainfall` in this simulation.
- **Right:** OOB predicted vs observed yield. Points near the dashed 1:1 line = good predictions. A wide scatter cloud or systematic curvature means the forest is struggling with some part of the range.
:::

::: {.civilbox}
**Why forests are the workhorse of geospatial ML:** They handle mixed units (m, %, mm, index), need no scaling, capture non-linear thresholds (floods are threshold phenomena), and give importance rankings that map directly onto factor maps used in susceptibility analysis.
:::

---

# Proximity and Probability Models

## K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)

### The idea in one line

To classify a new point, look at the $k$ closest training points and take a majority vote. Distance (Euclidean):

$$d(p, q) = \sqrt{(p_1-q_1)^2 + (p_2-q_2)^2 + \dots}$$

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** You send a soil sample to the lab and the lab tech says: *"It looks, feels and behaves like the samples from the three nearest boreholes — sandy."* No equation, just **similarity to known cases**. That is KNN. It is also exactly how engineers interpolate **groundwater levels between observation wells**.
:::

### Simulate a soil classification dataset

```{r knn-sim}
set.seed(61)
n_per <- 80
soil <- rbind(
  tibble(sand = rnorm(n_per, 72, 8), clay = rnorm(n_per, 8, 4), soil_type = "Sandy"),
  tibble(sand = rnorm(n_per, 45, 10), clay = rnorm(n_per, 25, 6), soil_type = "Loamy"),
  tibble(sand = rnorm(n_per, 20, 8), clay = rnorm(n_per, 55, 9), soil_type = "Clayey")
) %>%
  mutate(
    sand = pmin(pmax(round(sand), 0), 100),
    clay = pmin(pmax(round(clay), 0), 100)
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** A 240-row dataset with three soil classes, each described by sand% and clay%. Sandy soils have high sand, clayey soils have high clay, loamy sits in the middle. The `pmin`/`pmax` clipping keeps unrealistic percentages inside 0–100.
:::

### See the algorithm "think": neighborhoods of a new sample

```{r knn-concept, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.6, fig.cap="KNN in action: the dashed circle votes with k = 7 neighbors, the solid with k = 3."}
new_soil <- tibble(sand = 48, clay = 18)
d_new <- sqrt((soil$sand - new_soil$sand)^2 + (soil$clay - new_soil$clay)^2)
ord <- order(d_new)
k3 <- soil[ord[1:3], ]
k7 <- soil[ord[1:7], ]

circle <- function(cx, cy, r, n = 240) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  tibble(x = cx + r * cos(t), y = cy + r * sin(t))
}
c3 <- circle(
  new_soil$sand, new_soil$clay,
  max(sqrt((k3$sand - new_soil$sand)^2 + (k3$clay - new_soil$clay)^2)) + 2
)
c7 <- circle(
  new_soil$sand, new_soil$clay,
  max(sqrt((k7$sand - new_soil$sand)^2 + (k7$clay - new_soil$clay)^2)) + 2
)

soil_cols <- c(Sandy = "goldenrod1", Loamy = "forestgreen", Clayey = "brown3")

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = soil, aes(sand, clay, colour = soil_type), size = 1.8, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_path(data = c7, aes(x, y), colour = "grey30", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_path(data = c3, aes(x, y), colour = "grey10", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(
    data = k7, aes(sand, clay), shape = 21, fill = "white",
    colour = "black", size = 2.6
  ) +
  geom_point(data = new_soil, aes(sand, clay), shape = 17, size = 4.5) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 46, y = 4, size = 3.4,
    label = "New sample (triangle)\nk=3 votes: ?   k=7 votes: ?"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = soil_cols, name = "Soil class") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "K-nearest neighbors: classification by local vote",
    x = "Sand content (%)", y = "Clay content (%)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The black triangle is the new sample to classify. The two circles enclose its 3 and 7 nearest neighbours. **k = 3** votes only with the closest 3 dots — a "local" opinion. **k = 7** widens the circle, bringing in more neighbours — a "neighbourhood" opinion. Small k reacts to local noise; large k smooths out real structure. Section 6.4 shows how to choose k properly.
:::

### Decision boundaries: the effect of k

```{r knn-boundaries, fig.width=10.5, fig.height=3.9, fig.cap="Small k = wiggly, overfit boundaries; large k = smooth, possibly underfit. Same bias-variance tradeoff from Unit 3."}
grid_s <- expand.grid(
  sand = seq(0, 100, length.out = 150),
  clay = seq(0, 100, length.out = 150)
)

make_knn_grid <- function(k) {
  g <- grid_s
  g$pred <- knn(
    train = soil[, c("sand", "clay")],
    test = g[, c("sand", "clay")],
    cl = soil$soil_type, k = k
  )
  g$k <- sprintf("k = %d", k)
  g
}

bind_rows(make_knn_grid(1), make_knn_grid(7), make_knn_grid(25)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(sand, clay, fill = pred)) +
  geom_raster(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(
    data = soil,
    aes(x = sand, y = clay, colour = soil_type),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 0.9, alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = soil_cols, name = "Predicted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = soil_cols, name = "Actual") +
  facet_wrap(~k) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "KNN decision boundaries for different k",
    x = "Sand (%)", y = "Clay (%)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** Three KNN boundaries are shown for k = 1, 7, and 25. **k = 1** produces jagged, overfit boundaries that chase individual points — the bias-variance lesson from Unit 3 in action. **k = 25** produces smooth but possibly over-generic boundaries. **k = 7** is usually the sweet spot in problems this size.
:::

### Choosing k by validation

```{r knn-kcurve, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Accuracy vs k. Use odd k to avoid tied votes."}
set.seed(62)
idx_s <- sample(seq_len(nrow(soil)), 0.7 * nrow(soil))
soil_tr <- soil[idx_s, ]
soil_te <- soil[-idx_s, ]
ks <- seq(1, 31, by = 2)
acc_s <- sapply(ks, function(k) {
  p <- knn(
    train = soil_tr[, c("sand", "clay")],
    test = soil_te[, c("sand", "clay")],
    cl = soil_tr$soil_type, k = k
  )
  mean(p == soil_te$soil_type)
})
tibble(k = ks, accuracy = acc_s) %>%
  ggplot(aes(k, accuracy)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(colour = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = ks) +
  labs(
    title = "Choosing k: test accuracy curve",
    x = "k (number of neighbors)", y = "Test accuracy"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this curve:** The peak of the curve is the best k for *this dataset* — not a universal constant. Notice the drop at very small k (noise) and at very large k (over-smoothing). **Use odd k** for binary classification to avoid tied votes. Pick the k where the curve is both high *and* flat — a flat plateau means the choice is robust to small changes.
:::

### The scaling trap (very important!)

```{r knn-scaling}
raw_demo <- data.frame(area_m2 = c(800, 5000), age_yrs = c(10, 12))
dist(raw_demo) # area dominates: 4200 vs 2 !!!
dist(scale(raw_demo)) # after z-standardisation both features count
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this output:** The first distance is dominated by the `area_m2` difference (thousands) — the `age_yrs` difference (2) is invisible by comparison. The second distance, computed after z-standardising each column, gives both features equal weight. **This is why Unit 3's scaling lesson matters so much for KNN.**
:::

::: {.warnbox}
**Rule:** KNN uses raw distances, so **always scale features** (Unit 3 normalization!) when units differ — e.g., building area (m²) vs age (years), or rainfall (mm) vs slope (%).
:::

## Naive Bayes

### The idea in one line

Use **Bayes' theorem** with the *"naive"* assumption that features are independent within each class:

$$P(y \mid x_1, \dots, x_d) \propto P(y) \prod_{j=1}^{d} P(x_j \mid y)$$

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** A bridge inspector decides *"corrosion distress likely?"* by combining the **prior** (bridges of this age & coastal exposure fail often) with each **symptom separately** (rust stains? spalling? drainage blocked?) without modeling interactions between symptoms. Crude but fast — and surprisingly strong as a screening tool.
:::

```{r nb-ellipse, fig.width=7.8, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="'Naive' means we pretend the tilted (correlated) cloud is axis-aligned. Loss of realism, gain of speed."}
ellipse_pts <- function(cx, cy, a, b, theta = 0, n = 240) {
  t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n)
  tibble(
    x = cx + a * cos(t) * cos(theta) - b * sin(t) * sin(theta),
    y = cy + a * cos(t) * sin(theta) + b * sin(t) * cos(theta)
  )
}
truth <- ellipse_pts(85, 0.68, 26, 0.11, pi / 6)
naive <- ellipse_pts(85, 0.68, 26, 0.11, 0)
ggplot() +
  geom_path(
    data = truth, aes(x, y), colour = "firebrick",
    linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "solid"
  ) +
  geom_path(
    data = naive, aes(x, y), colour = "grey30",
    linewidth = 1.1, linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 85, y = 0.86, size = 3.4,
    label = "dashed = Naive Bayes assumption\nsolid = true correlated cloud"
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = "What 'naive' means: features treated as independent",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)", y = "Soil wetness (index)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The solid red ellipse is the *true* joint distribution of rainfall and soil wetness in the flood class — they are correlated (wet ground + heavy rain come together). The dashed grey ellipse is the naive approximation — Naive Bayes pretends the axes are independent, drawing an axis-aligned cloud. It loses the tilt but gains computational speed and simplicity.
:::

### Simulate a flood-day dataset

```{r nb-sim}
set.seed(71)
nb_data <- rbind(
  tibble(rainfall = rnorm(350, 25, 12), soil_wetness = rnorm(350, 0.30, 0.12), flood_day = "no"),
  tibble(rainfall = rnorm(150, 85, 20), soil_wetness = rnorm(150, 0.70, 0.10), flood_day = "yes")
) %>%
  mutate(
    rainfall = round(pmax(rainfall, 0), 1),
    soil_wetness = round(pmin(pmax(soil_wetness, 0), 1), 2),
    flood_day = factor(flood_day, levels = c("no", "yes"))
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** 500 days split into two classes — 350 non-flood and 150 flood days. Flood days are characterised by higher rainfall and higher soil wetness. This is a deliberately **imbalanced** dataset (30% positives), which is realistic for flood events and exactly the case where a naive accuracy metric would mislead.
:::

```{r nb-density, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Class-conditional distributions: Naive Bayes summarizes each feature per class with a mean and sd (Gaussian NB)."}
p1 <- ggplot(nb_data, aes(rainfall, fill = flood_day)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45) +
  labs(title = "Rainfall by flood day", x = "Rainfall (mm)")
p2 <- ggplot(nb_data, aes(soil_wetness, fill = flood_day)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45) +
  labs(title = "Soil wetness by flood day", x = "Soil wetness index")
p1 | p2
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read these density plots:** Each panel shows the *class-conditional* distribution of one feature. The further apart the two coloured curves, the more useful that feature is to the classifier. Both curves are visibly separated here — rainfall more so than wetness — which predicts a well-performing Naive Bayes model. **Gaussian NB** summarises each curve with just a mean and a standard deviation.
:::

### Fit, inspect, predict

```{r nb-fit}
set.seed(72)
nb_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(nb_data)), 0.7 * nrow(nb_data))
nb_train <- nb_data[nb_idx, ]
nb_test <- nb_data[-nb_idx, ]

nb_fit <- naiveBayes(flood_day ~ rainfall + soil_wetness, data = nb_train)
nb_fit # prints the prior P(y) and per-class means/sds — the whole model!
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the printed model:** The output is the *entire trained model* in a few lines. **`A-priori probabilities`** = the class priors (roughly 70/30). The two blocks below print the mean and standard deviation of each feature, split by class. That is all Naive Bayes stores — tiny, fast, interpretable. Contrast that with 500 decision trees or a deep neural network.
:::

```{r nb-posterior}
predict(nb_fit, newdata = tibble(rainfall = 60, soil_wetness = 0.55), type = "raw")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the posterior output:** Two numbers are printed — the posterior probability of each class for a day with 60 mm rainfall and 0.55 wetness. The larger one wins. That transparancy — showing both probabilities — is why NB is often used as a fast screening tool before a heavier model is deployed.
:::

```{r nb-region, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.2, fig.cap="Naive Bayes decision regions with the held-out test points."}
nb_grid <- expand.grid(
  rainfall = seq(0, 160, length.out = 180),
  soil_wetness = seq(0, 1, length.out = 180)
)
nb_grid$pred <- predict(nb_fit, newdata = nb_grid)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = nb_grid, aes(rainfall, soil_wetness, fill = pred), alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_point(data = nb_test, aes(rainfall, soil_wetness, colour = flood_day), size = 1.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(no = "dodgerblue", yes = "firebrick"), name = "Predicted") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(no = "navy", yes = "red"), name = "Actual") +
  labs(
    title = "Naive Bayes: flood-day decision regions",
    x = "Rainfall (mm)", y = "Soil wetness index"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** The background colour is the predicted class at each point on the (rainfall, wetness) plane. The boundary between blue and red regions is the *decision surface* — a straight-ish line because NB is (essentially) a linear classifier in this feature space. Points are the held-out test set: blue = no flood, red = flood. The model is doing well when red points land in red regions.
:::

```{r nb-acc}
pred_nb <- predict(nb_fit, newdata = nb_test)
sprintf("Naive Bayes test accuracy = %.1f%%", 100 * mean(pred_nb == nb_test$flood_day))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this number:** This is the *test accuracy* — how often the model got the right class on data it never saw. Given how separated the two distributions are, accuracy above 90% is expected. **But remember Unit 3's warning:** for rare, dangerous events like floods, always check recall next to accuracy.
:::

# Clustering Techniques for Regional Analysis

::: {.civilbox}
**Why clustering for a civil engineer?** Planning does not start with labeled data — it starts with *"give me homogeneous zones."* Water-supply design zones, transport fare zones, maintenance contract packages, landslide-prone vs stable regions: all are **unsupervised grouping** problems. Here the labels do not exist; the algorithm invents them.
:::

## K-Means

### The idea in one line

Choose $K$ centroids, assign each point to the nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat — minimizing:

$$\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{x_i \in C_k} \lVert x_i - \mu_k \rVert^2$$

### Simulate 360 settlements (urban / suburban / rural)

```{r km-sim}
set.seed(81)
n_zone <- 120
regions <- rbind(
  tibble(pop_density = rnorm(n_zone, 8000, 1500), ndvi = rnorm(n_zone, 0.25, 0.06), zone = "Urban core"),
  tibble(pop_density = rnorm(n_zone, 2800, 700), ndvi = rnorm(n_zone, 0.45, 0.07), zone = "Suburban"),
  tibble(pop_density = rnorm(n_zone, 500, 180), ndvi = rnorm(n_zone, 0.65, 0.06), zone = "Rural")
) %>%
  mutate(
    pop_density = round(pmax(pop_density, 50)),
    ndvi = round(pmin(pmax(ndvi, 0.02), 0.95), 3)
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** 360 simulated settlements, each described by population density and NDVI (greenness). Three true zones exist in the simulation — dense urban cores with low NDVI, mid-density suburbs, and sparse rural areas with high NDVI. **The clustering algorithm will not see these labels** — its job is to rediscover them from the raw coordinates alone.
:::

### Choosing K: elbow method + silhouette

```{r km-elbow, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=4.3, fig.cap="Elbow (left) — read it like a load-deflection curve: the 'yield point' is K = 3. Silhouette (right) agrees."}
X <- regions %>%
  select(pop_density, ndvi) %>%
  scale()
ks <- 1:10
wss <- sapply(ks, function(k) kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss)
avg_sil <- sapply(ks[-1], function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(X, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  mean(silhouette(km$cluster, dist(X))[, 3])
})

p_elbow <- tibble(k = ks, wss = wss) %>%
  ggplot(aes(k, wss)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Elbow method", x = "K", y = "Total within-cluster SS")

p_sil <- tibble(k = ks[-1], sil = avg_sil) %>%
  ggplot(aes(k, sil)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "darkgreen") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Average silhouette width", x = "K", y = "Mean silhouette")

p_elbow | p_sil
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read these two plots:**

- **Elbow (left):** WSS (total within-cluster sum of squares) always decreases as K grows — the trick is to find the *knee* where improvement suddenly slows. That knee is usually the right K. Here it sits near K = 3.
- **Silhouette (right):** A measure of how well each point fits its own cluster (range −1 to +1). Higher is better. The peak usually agrees with the elbow — a reassuring cross-check.

**Never trust one method alone.** When both agree, the choice of K is on solid ground.
:::

### Final clustering and interpretation

```{r km-final, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="K-means zones (K = 3) with centroids. The algorithm never saw the true labels!"}
km3 <- kmeans(X, centers = 3, nstart = 25)
regions$cluster <- factor(km3$cluster)

centroids <- sweep(
  sweep(km3$centers, 2, attr(X, "scaled:scale"), `*`),
  2, attr(X, "scaled:center"), `+`
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(1:3))

ggplot(regions, aes(pop_density, ndvi, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(
    data = centroids, aes(pop_density, ndvi, colour = cluster),
    shape = 18, size = 6
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Cluster") +
  labs(
    title = "K-means regional zoning (diamonds = centroids)",
    x = "Population density (per km²)", y = "NDVI (green cover)"
  ) +
  coord_equal()
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** Each point is a settlement, coloured by the cluster the algorithm assigned. Diamonds are the three centroids — the "representative" point of each cluster. Notice how three distinct bands emerge, matching the true urban/suburban/rural split — even though the algorithm never saw the true labels. **The algorithm's job stops here; your job is to *name* the clusters.**
:::

```{r km-interp}
regions %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_pop = round(mean(pop_density)),
    mean_ndvi = round(mean(ndvi), 2)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_pop))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this summary:** For each cluster the table shows how many settlements, the mean population density, and the mean NDVI. **The cluster with the highest mean_pop and lowest mean_ndvi is your urban core; the one with the lowest density and highest greenness is rural.** Naming clusters is human work — the algorithm only gives numbers.
:::

```{r km-truth}
table(Cluster = regions$cluster, True_zone = regions$zone)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this cross-tab:** Rows are K-means clusters, columns are the *true* labels used in the simulation. A perfect clustering would put all counts on a single diagonal — one cluster per true zone. Real clustering usually has a few misassignments at the boundaries between zones, which is normal.
:::

## Hierarchical Clustering

### The idea in one line

Start with every point as its own cluster; repeatedly **merge the two closest clusters** (agglomerative). "Closest" depends on the **linkage** rule. The result is a **dendrogram** — cut it at a height to get K clusters.

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** A dendrogram is like the **Work Breakdown Structure** of a megaproject: individual activities merge into work packages, packages into sections, sections into the project. Cutting the tree at any level gives you a different contract-packaging granularity.
:::

```{r hc-dendro, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="Ward dendrogram of 45 settlements; boxes show the K = 3 cut."}
set.seed(82)
h_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(regions)), 45)
h_data <- regions[h_idx, c("pop_density", "ndvi", "zone")]
h_scaled <- scale(h_data[, c("pop_density", "ndvi")])

hc_ward <- hclust(dist(h_scaled), method = "ward.D2")
plot(hc_ward,
  main = "Hierarchical clustering of settlements (Ward linkage)",
  sub = "", xlab = "", cex = 0.6, labels = FALSE
)
rect.hclust(hc_ward, k = 3, border = c("firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen"))

m <- length(hc_ward$height)
k_cut <- 3
h_cut <- mean(hc_ward$height[(m - k_cut + 1):(m - k_cut + 2)])
abline(h = h_cut, lty = 2, col = "red")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the dendrogram:** Each vertical leaf at the bottom is one settlement. The height at which two leaves join = the "distance" at which those clusters merged. **Short joining heights = very similar; tall joining heights = dissimilar.** The three coloured rectangles show a cut at K = 3, which produces three clusters. The dashed horizontal line is the cut height.
:::

### Linkage matters: same data, four dendrograms

```{r hc-linkages, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=7, fig.cap="Single linkage chains; complete cuts compact balls; Ward balances sizes. Choice of linkage is an engineering judgement."}
methods <- c("single", "complete", "average", "ward.D2")
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (mm in methods) {
  hc <- hclust(dist(h_scaled), method = mm)
  plot(hc,
    main = paste("Linkage:", mm), sub = "", xlab = "",
    cex = 0.55, labels = FALSE
  )
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read these four dendrograms:**

- **Single linkage:** chains clusters together by their closest pair — tends to produce long, "stringy" clusters.
- **Complete linkage:** merges clusters by their *farthest* pair — produces compact, roughly equal-size balls.
- **Average linkage:** a compromise — the average distance between all pairs.
- **Ward:** minimises the increase in within-cluster variance — the most popular default for numeric data.

**The choice is engineering judgement**: if you want equal-size planning zones, use Ward. If you want to detect chained anomalies, single linkage exposes them.
:::

```{r hc-scatter, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5, fig.cap="The 45 settlements coloured by hierarchical clusters — same geography as K-means, different route."}
h_data$hc_cluster <- factor(cutree(hc_ward, k = 3))
ggplot(h_data, aes(pop_density, ndvi, colour = hc_cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(name = "Cluster") +
  labs(
    title = "Settlements grouped by hierarchical clustering",
    x = "Population density (per km²)", y = "NDVI"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this figure:** Same as the K-means plot, but the clusters come from hierarchical clustering instead. On a dataset this clean, both methods tend to find the same three zones. On messier data they can disagree — which is a signal to examine the borderline cases manually.
:::
