# Geospatial Data Structures

## Raster vs Vector — The Two Languages of Maps

| | **Raster** | **Vector** |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Grid of equal cells, each holding a value | Points, lines, polygons with coordinates |
| Examples | Satellite images, DEMs, rainfall surfaces | Pipes, roads, parcel boundaries, boreholes |
| Resolution | Cell size (e.g., 30 m Landsat, 10 m Sentinel) | Unlimited (true coordinates) |
| Strengths | Continuous surfaces, image processing, fast overlay | Precise geometry, topology, attributes per feature |
| In R | `terra` (SpatRaster) | `sf` (simple features) |

```{r geo-rv-concept, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Left: raster = cells. Right: vector = points (wells), line (pipe), polygon (parcel)."}
grid_df <- expand.grid(x = 1:8, y = 1:8)
set.seed(91)
grid_df$value <- sample(1:5, nrow(grid_df),
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(.35, .3, .2, .1, .05)
)
p_raster <- ggplot(grid_df, aes(x, y, fill = factor(value))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako", guide = "none") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "RASTER — grid of cells",
    subtitle = "satellite images, DEMs, rainfall surfaces"
  )

pts_df <- tibble(x = c(2.2, 3.5, 5.1, 6.8), y = c(2.5, 4.2, 3.1, 5.5))
line_df <- tibble(
  x = seq(1, 7, length.out = 60),
  y = 1.2 + 0.35 * sin(seq(1, 7, length.out = 60) * 1.4)
)
poly_df <- tibble(
  x = c(5.2, 7.2, 7.6, 5.6, 5.2),
  y = c(5.6, 5.9, 7.0, 6.6, 5.6)
)
p_vector <- ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = poly_df, aes(x, y), fill = "palegreen3",
    alpha = 0.85, colour = "grey20"
  ) +
  geom_path(data = line_df, aes(x, y), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(data = pts_df, aes(x, y), colour = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(1, 8), ylim = c(1, 8)) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "VECTOR — points, lines, polygons",
    subtitle = "wells, pipelines, parcels"
  )

p_raster | p_vector
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the two panels:**

- **Left (Raster):** The world is chopped into a grid of equal cells, each holding one value. Satellite images, elevation models, and rainfall surfaces are all rasters.
- **Right (Vector):** The world is described by precise geometry — points (wells), lines (pipes), and polygons (parcels). Each feature can carry its own attributes.

**In practice you will use both.** A flood susceptibility workflow might use a DEM raster, a river polyline vector, and a set of observed-flood point locations. `terra` handles the first; `sf` handles the other two.
:::

## Rasters in R with `terra`

```{r geo-raster, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="A digital elevation model as a SpatRaster (100 m cells)."}
set.seed(92)
r100 <- rast(
  nrows = 50, ncols = 50, xmin = 0, xmax = 5000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 5000, crs = "EPSG:32643"
)
xy_r <- xyFromCell(r100, 1:ncell(r100))
elev_r <- 200 + 100 * sin(xy_r[, "x"] / 1500) + 60 * cos(xy_r[, "y"] / 1200) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_r), 0, 5)
values(r100) <- elev_r
names(r100) <- "elevation_m"
plot(r100, col = viridis(100), main = "DEM raster — 100 m cells")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this map:** The colour scale shows elevation from low (dark) to high (yellow). Each grid cell is 100 m × 100 m. The `crs = "EPSG:32643"` sets the coordinate reference system (UTM zone 43N) — the layer is geographically anchored. **This is the kind of object you would download from Bhuvan or USGS and immediately read into R with `rast("dem.tif")`.**
:::

### Resolution matters — coarsening the mesh

```{r geo-resolution, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Aggregating a raster = coarsening the mesh. Fine cells capture detail; coarse cells are faster but blurrier."}
r25 <- aggregate(r100, fact = 2) # 200 m cells
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(r100, col = viridis(100), main = "100 m cells (fine)")
plot(r25, col = viridis(100), main = "200 m cells (coarse)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this comparison:** The left raster has 100 m cells; the right has 200 m cells (each new cell is the average of 4 old ones). The coarser version is faster to process and smaller to store, but loses fine detail — exactly like using a coarser mesh in FEA. **Choose resolution based on what decisions you need to support**, not on what looks nicest.
:::

## Vectors in R with `sf`

```{r geo-vector, fig.width=9, fig.height=5, fig.cap="An sf map: monitoring wells (points), a water pipeline (line), a building footprint (polygon)."}
wells <- st_as_sf(
  tibble(
    name = c("W1", "W2", "W3", "W4"),
    x = c(1000, 2500, 3600, 4400),
    y = c(1200, 3000, 2200, 4100)
  ),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32643
)

pipe_line <- st_sfc(
  st_linestring(cbind(c(200, 1800, 3200, 4800), c(4000, 3200, 3600, 1000))),
  crs = 32643
)

building <- st_sfc(
  st_polygon(list(cbind(
    c(2600, 3400, 3400, 2600, 2600),
    c(1200, 1200, 2000, 2000, 1200)
  ))),
  crs = 32643
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = building, fill = "wheat2", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_sf(data = pipe_line, colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_sf(data = wells, shape = 21, fill = "firebrick", size = 3.2) +
  geom_sf_text(data = wells, aes(label = name), nudge_y = 200, size = 3.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Vector data with sf",
    subtitle = "points = wells | line = pipeline | polygon = building"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this vector map:** All three geometry types are shown together — points (wells, red dots), lines (pipeline, blue curve), and a polygon (building, tan). Each carries a **CRS**, without which geometry is meaningless. `geom_sf()` is the ggplot2 bridge that draws any `sf` object without extra work.
:::

A taste of spatial analysis in one line — distance of each well to the pipeline (useful for **right-of-way compliance**):

```{r geo-distance}
st_distance(wells, pipe_line)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this output:** A matrix of distances in metres (because the CRS is a metric projection, not lat/lon degrees). Each row = one well; the single column = distance to the pipeline. **Real use:** the well with the smallest distance is the one that violates right-of-way and needs to be relocated.
:::

::: {.tipbox}
**Real data at home:** read a GeoTIFF with `rast("dem.tif")`, a shapefile or GeoPackage with `st_read("roads.shp")`. Free sources: Bhuvan (ISRO), USGS EarthExplorer, Copernicus Open Access, OpenStreetMap.
:::

---

# Satellite Image Processing

### Simulate a 4-band image (Red, Green, Blue, NIR)

Each land-cover type has a **spectral signature** — the key physics: **vegetation reflects NIR strongly** (leaf structure) but absorbs red (photosynthesis). That contrast is what NDVI exploits.

```{r sat-sim}
set.seed(101)
nr <- 100
nc <- 100
img <- rast(
  nrows = nr, ncols = nc, xmin = 0, xmax = 1000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 1000, nlyrs = 4
)
xy_img <- xyFromCell(img, 1:ncell(img))
colnames(xy_img) <- c("x", "y")

river_c <- 420 + 110 * sin(xy_img[, "x"] / 140)
dist_riv <- abs(xy_img[, "y"] - river_c)

land_class <- ifelse(dist_riv < 28, "water",
  ifelse(xy_img[, "x"] > 620 & xy_img[, "y"] > 620, "urban",
    ifelse(rnorm(ncell(img), 0, 45) < -22, "bare", "vegetation")
  )
)

sig_mat <- matrix(
  c( # rows = bands, cols = classes
    .06, .08, .30, .25, # Red
    .09, .16, .34, .25, # Green
    .13, .08, .30, .25, # Blue
    .03, .46, .38, .21
  ), # NIR
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(
    c("red", "green", "blue", "nir"),
    c("water", "vegetation", "bare", "urban")
  )
)

set.seed(102)
band_mat <- t(sig_mat[, land_class]) +
  matrix(rnorm(4 * ncell(img), 0, 0.015), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)

values(img) <- band_mat
names(img) <- c("red", "green", "blue", "nir")
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** A 4-layer raster with 10 000 cells. Each cell has a red, green, blue, and near-infrared reflectance value. The dataset was built by assigning each cell one of four land-cover classes (water, vegetation, bare soil, urban), then giving it the appropriate spectral signature. **Real satellite imagery works exactly this way** — bands are reflectance values, not colours.
:::

```{r sat-composites, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="True colour (left) vs false colour composite (right): healthy vegetation glows red in the NIR band."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plotRGB(img,
  r = 1, g = 2, b = 3, stretch = "lin",
  main = "True colour (R, G, B)"
)
plotRGB(img,
  r = 4, g = 1, b = 2, stretch = "lin",
  main = "False colour (NIR, R, G)"
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the two composites:**

- **True colour (left):** Bands 1, 2, 3 mapped to R, G, B — what your eyes would see. Water is dark blue-black, vegetation is greenish, urban is grey.
- **False colour (right):** Band 4 (NIR) mapped to Red. Because vegetation strongly reflects NIR, **all healthy vegetation glows red** in this composite. This is the standard trick every remote-sensing analyst uses to make vegetation pop out visually.
:::

### NDVI — the most-used vegetation index on Earth

$$NDVI = \frac{NIR - Red}{NIR + Red}$$

```{r sat-ndvi, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="NDVI map: water ≈ 0 or below, bare soil ≈ 0.1-0.2, vegetation > 0.3."}
ndvi <- (img$nir - img$red) / (img$nir + img$red)
plot(ndvi,
  col = viridis(100),
  main = "NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red)"
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the NDVI map:** Yellow-green areas = high NDVI = healthy vegetation. Dark areas = low NDVI = water, bare soil, or built-up surfaces. The river corridor running across the image shows up as a dark line. **Values range from −1 to +1** by definition, but real land surfaces almost always sit between 0 and 1.
:::

```{r sat-ndvi-hist, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.9, fig.cap="NDVI histogram: the dashed line (0.3) is a simple threshold rule to build a vegetation mask."}
ndvi_vals <- values(ndvi)[, 1]
tibble(ndvi = ndvi_vals) %>%
  ggplot(aes(ndvi)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "forestgreen", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(
    title = "NDVI distribution — thresholding is a 1-class classifier",
    x = "NDVI", y = "Cell count"
  )

rcl_v <- matrix(c(
  -1, 0.3, 0,
  0.3, 1, 1
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
veg_mask <- classify(ndvi, rcl_v)
plot(veg_mask,
  col = c("grey85", "forestgreen"),
  main = "Vegetation mask (NDVI > 0.3)"
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the histogram and mask:** The histogram shows the distribution of NDVI across all cells. The dashed line at 0.3 is a *chosen threshold* — anything above it is declared vegetation. **The resulting binary map (bottom) is a classifier** — a very simple one, but a classifier nonetheless. Real ML work often begins with such a threshold as a baseline before trying something smarter.
:::

::: {.civilbox}
**Where you will use this:** crop area estimation (agriculture engineering), pre/post-monsoon greenness change (flood damage), corridor vegetation clearance auditing (highways), urban green-space equity (planning). Real missions: **Landsat 8/9 (30 m), Sentinel-2 (10 m, free)**.
:::

---

# Remote Sensing Integration: GIS + AI Fusion

## The Workflow That Runs Modern Geospatial ML

```{r fusion-workflow, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="GIS + AI fusion: extract table-like features from map layers, learn, then predict back onto the map."}
steps <- tibble(
  x = 1:5,
  label = c(
    "Geospatial layers\n(raster + vector)",
    "extract() features\nat training points",
    "Machine learning\nmodel (e.g., RF)",
    "predict() on the\nwhole raster",
    "Susceptibility map\n→ decisions"
  ),
  fill = c("#4C72B0", "#55A868", "#C44E52", "#8172B2", "#CCB974")
)
ggplot() +
  geom_rect(
    data = steps, aes(
      xmin = x - 0.42, xmax = x + 0.42,
      ymin = 0, ymax = 1.4, fill = fill
    ),
    colour = "grey25"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = steps, aes(x, y = 0.7, label = label), size = 3,
    fontface = "bold", colour = "white", lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = tibble(x = 1:4, xend = 2:5),
    aes(x = x + 0.45, xend = xend - 0.45, y = 0.7, yend = 0.7),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
    linewidth = 0.8, colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  xlim(0.3, 5.7) +
  ylim(-0.2, 1.6) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "GIS + AI fusion in five steps")
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the workflow:** Five steps, left to right. **Step 1:** gather raster and vector layers (DEM, rainfall, NDVI, rivers). **Step 2:** at each labelled training point, extract the pixel value of every layer into a table row — this is the map→table translator. **Step 3:** train any ML classifier on the table. **Step 4:** feed the *entire* raster stack back to the trained model — this is the table→map translator. **Step 5:** classify the resulting probabilities into planning zones.
:::

::: {.keybox}
**The fusion secret:** a GIS sees a *map*; an ML algorithm sees a *table*. `terra::extract()` is the translator **map → table**; `terra::predict()` is the translator **table → map**. Learn these two functions and you can attach any classifier to any landscape.
:::

## Full Demonstration: Flood Susceptibility Mapping End-to-End

### Step 1 — build the geospatial knowledge base (4 terrain layers)

```{r fusion-terrain, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=6.6, fig.cap="The four environmental layers that will become ML features."}
set.seed(111)
terr <- rast(
  nrows = 80, ncols = 80, xmin = 0, xmax = 8000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 8000, nlyrs = 4
)
xy_t <- xyFromCell(terr, 1:ncell(terr))
colnames(xy_t) <- c("x", "y")

elevation_t <- 250 + 130 * sin(xy_t[, "x"] / 2600) +
  90 * cos(xy_t[, "y"] / 2100) + rnorm(nrow(xy_t), 0, 4)
slope_t <- pmax(0.5, 6 + 7 * sin(xy_t[, "x"] / 1700) *
  cos(xy_t[, "y"] / 1500) + rnorm(nrow(xy_t), 0, 0.6))
rain_t <- 950 + 320 * sin((xy_t[, "x"] + xy_t[, "y"]) / 4200) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_t), 0, 15)
ndvi_t <- pmin(pmax(0.62 - 0.00004 * xy_t[, "x"] -
  0.00002 * xy_t[, "y"] +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_t), 0, 0.06), 0.05), 0.9)

values(terr) <- cbind(elevation_t, slope_t, rain_t, ndvi_t)
names(terr) <- c("elevation", "slope", "rainfall", "ndvi")
plot(terr)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the four panels:** Each panel is one environmental layer across the same 8 × 8 km landscape. `elevation` has smooth hills; `slope` varies sinusoidally; `rainfall` has a gradient; `ndvi` (greenness) is highest in the lower-left corner. **These four rasters together are the model's inputs** — every cell will be a training or prediction example.
:::

### Step 2 — extract features at 400 training points (map → table)

```{r fusion-extract}
set.seed(112)
n_train <- 400
cells_t <- sample(ncell(terr), n_train)
pts_xy <- as_tibble(xyFromCell(terr, cells_t))
env_t <- as_tibble(extract(terr, cells_t))

# simulate field observations of flooding
logit_t <- 5 - 0.020 * env_t$elevation - 0.25 * env_t$slope +
  0.004 * env_t$rainfall - 2.0 * env_t$ndvi
flood_obs <- factor(ifelse(rbinom(n_train, 1, plogis(logit_t)) == 1,
  "yes", "no"
), levels = c("no", "yes"))

train_tab <- bind_cols(pts_xy, env_t, tibble(flood = flood_obs))
head(train_tab)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this table:** Each row is one sampled point on the map, with its x/y coordinates, the extracted value of every environmental layer at that point, and the observed flood label. **This table is what the ML model sees.** The map has disappeared; only numbers remain. The same table shape works whether you have 400 points or 40,000.
:::

### Step 3 — train the model on the table

```{r fusion-rf}
rf_terr <- randomForest(flood ~ elevation + slope + rainfall + ndvi,
  data = train_tab, ntree = 500
)
rf_terr
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the printed forest:** Standard random-forest output — number of trees, OOB confusion matrix, and per-class OOB error. The low OOB error tells you the model has learned a real signal. **This is the same output format you saw in Section 5** — the workflow generalises: the terrain layers just became columns of a table.
:::

### Step 4 — predict on the whole raster (table → map)

```{r fusion-map, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5.6, fig.cap="The final susceptibility map — every cell of the landscape scored by the forest. Black dots = observed flood points."}
pred_fun <- function(model, newdata) {
  predict(model, newdata = newdata, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
}
flood_prob <- predict(terr, rf_terr, fun = pred_fun, na.rm = TRUE)

plot(flood_prob,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "Spectral", rev = TRUE),
  main = "Predicted flood susceptibility (GIS + ML fusion)"
)
points(xy_t[cells_t, ],
  col = ifelse(flood_obs == "yes", "black", "grey60"),
  pch = 19, cex = 0.5
)
legend("topright", c("Observed flood", "No flood"),
  col = c("black", "grey60"), pch = 19, cex = 0.8, bty = "n"
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this map:** The colour scale runs from low (blue) to high (red) predicted flood probability. **Every pixel of the landscape now has a prediction** — even those we never sampled. Black dots are observed flood points; grey are non-flood. A well-trained model places black dots predominantly in the red/yellow zones and grey dots in the blue zones.
:::

### Step 5 — convert probabilities into planning zones

```{r fusion-zones, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="Zoned susceptibility map — this is the layer that goes into the land-use plan."}
rcl_f <- matrix(c(
  0, 0.2, 1,
  0.2, 0.4, 2,
  0.4, 0.6, 3,
  0.6, 0.8, 4,
  0.8, 1, 5
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
flood_class <- classify(flood_prob, rcl_f)
plot(flood_class,
  col = c("lightblue", "skyblue", "khaki", "orange", "firebrick"),
  main = "Flood susceptibility zones (1 = very low … 5 = very high)"
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this zoned map:** The continuous probability map has been collapsed into five discrete classes — very low, low, moderate, high, very high. **Discrete classes are what policy and planning need.** A town plan says "no construction in zone 5," not "no construction where probability > 0.83." The thresholds (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8) are an engineering choice — you can also use quantile breaks for equal-area zones.
:::

::: {.civilbox}
**You have just performed the exact workflow of published flood/landslide susceptibility papers** — only with simulated data. Swap the simulated stack for real Sentinel-2 + DEM derivatives and the code barely changes.
:::

---

# Advanced Mapping Applications

## Urban Heat Island (UHI) Analysis

**The phenomenon:** cities replace vegetation and water with concrete and asphalt → they absorb more solar radiation and evaporate less → the city core runs several degrees hotter than its rural surroundings.

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil engineering relevance:** pavement materials, building density, and green-cover mandates are *design levers* on city temperature. UHI studies guide cool-roof codes, park placement, and heat-action plans.
:::

```{r uhi-sim}
set.seed(121)
nr_u <- 120
nc_u <- 120
uhi <- rast(
  nrows = nr_u, ncols = nc_u, xmin = 0, xmax = 12000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 12000, nlyrs = 2
)
xy_u <- xyFromCell(uhi, 1:ncell(uhi))
colnames(xy_u) <- c("x", "y")
d_center <- sqrt((xy_u[, "x"] - 6000)^2 + (xy_u[, "y"] - 6000)^2)

ndvi_u <- pmin(pmax(0.7 - 0.65 * exp(-d_center^2 / (2 * 2600^2)) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_u), 0, 0.05), 0.02), 0.9)
lst_u <- 30 + 8.5 * exp(-d_center^2 / (2 * 2500^2)) -
  6 * (ndvi_u - 0.3) + rnorm(nrow(xy_u), 0, 0.4)

values(uhi) <- cbind(lst_u, ndvi_u)
names(uhi) <- c("LST_C", "NDVI")
```

```{r uhi-map, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Simulated land-surface temperature: a hot core over a cooler rural halo — the classic UHI bullseye."}
plot(uhi$LST_C,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "Inferno"),
  main = "Land Surface Temperature (°C) — urban heat island"
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this map:** The colour scale is land-surface temperature. Note the **bullseye pattern** — the brightest (hottest) area is the city centre, surrounded by cooler rural pixels. The temperature difference between the two is the **UHI intensity** — typically 3–8 °C in real cities.
:::

### The transect: temperature along an east–west line

```{r uhi-transect, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="UHI profile across the city — read it like a longitudinal section through a heat 'dome'."}
dy <- abs(xy_u[, "y"] - 6000)
idx_row <- which(dy == min(dy))
tran <- tibble(
  x = xy_u[idx_row, "x"],
  lst = values(uhi$LST_C)[idx_row, 1]
) %>%
  group_by(x) %>%
  summarise(lst = mean(lst)) %>%
  arrange(x)

rural_base <- mean(lst_u[d_center > 5500])
uhi_int <- max(lst_u) - rural_base

ggplot(tran, aes(x, lst)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = rural_base, linetype = "dashed", colour = "forestgreen") +
  annotate("text",
    x = 800, y = rural_base + 0.6, colour = "forestgreen",
    size = 3.4, label = "rural baseline"
  ) +
  annotate("text",
    x = 6000, y = max(tran$lst) - 0.3, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold",
    colour = "firebrick",
    label = sprintf("UHI intensity ≈ %.1f °C", uhi_int)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "E-W temperature transect through the city",
    x = "Distance from western boundary (m)", y = "LST (°C)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the transect:** The curve shows temperature as you walk east across the city. The dashed green line is the rural baseline (average temperature far from the centre). The bump in the middle is the urban heat island. **The peak height above the baseline is the UHI intensity** — the number you would quote to a city planner.
:::

### The green-cooling effect: NDVI vs LST

```{r uhi-ndvi, fig.width=7.2, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Every unit of vegetation buys measurable cooling — quantify the slope and you can price a new park."}
tibble(ndvi = ndvi_u, lst = lst_u) %>%
  ggplot(aes(ndvi, lst)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "darkgreen", size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Green cooling: NDVI vs land surface temperature",
    subtitle = "Regression slope = °C of cooling per unit of NDVI",
    x = "NDVI", y = "LST (°C)"
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this scatter:** Each point is a pixel. The negative slope of the fitted line tells you that greener pixels are cooler pixels. **The slope's magnitude is directly useful**: a slope of −5 means that increasing NDVI by 1 unit cools the surface by 5 °C. That number is what lets you estimate how much temperature relief a proposed new park would provide.
:::

::: {.tipbox}
**Real workflow:** download Landsat 8/9 thermal band → convert DN to LST (radiance → brightness temp → emissivity correction) → compute NDVI from bands 4/5 → reproduce this exact analysis for your own city in QGIS or R.
:::

## Landslide Susceptibility Mapping

**The standard practice:** build an *inventory* of observed landslides, relate them to *conditioning factors* (slope, rainfall, geology, land cover), fit a model, and extrapolate the hazard over the whole terrain.

```{r ls-sim}
set.seed(131)
n_ls <- 500
land <- tibble(
  slope     = round(runif(n_ls, 2, 40), 1),
  rainfall  = round(runif(n_ls, 700, 2200), 0),
  elevation = round(runif(n_ls, 100, 900), 0),
  ndvi      = round(runif(n_ls, 0.05, 0.85), 2),
  rock_soft = sample(c(0, 1), n_ls, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))
) %>%
  mutate(
    logit_ls = -4 + 0.07 * slope + 0.0014 * rainfall -
      0.0012 * elevation - 1.0 * ndvi + 1.2 * rock_soft,
    landslide = factor(ifelse(rbinom(n_ls, 1, plogis(logit_ls)) == 1,
      "yes", "no"
    ), levels = c("no", "yes"))
  )
mean(land$landslide == "yes")
```

::: {.readbox}
**What you are seeing:** A 500-site landslide inventory. Each site has five conditioning factors and a binary landslide label. The final number is the base rate of landslides — typically 5–15% in real inventories, matching the simulated result.
:::

```{r ls-fit}
ls_fit <- glm(landslide ~ slope + rainfall + elevation + ndvi + rock_soft,
  family = binomial, data = land
)
tibble(
  term = names(coef(ls_fit)),
  odds_ratio = round(exp(coef(ls_fit)), 3)
)
```

::: {.readbox}
**Reading the odds ratios:** Each +1% of slope multiplies landslide odds by ~$e^{0.07} \approx 1.07$; soft rock multiplies them by ~3.3; dense vegetation (NDVI) *protects* (OR < 1). **Positive OR = the factor increases hazard; negative OR = protective.** This is exactly how susceptibility factor analyses are reported in journals.
:::

### Predict the whole terrain

```{r ls-terrain, include=FALSE}
set.seed(132)
ls_terr <- rast(
  nrows = 100, ncols = 100, xmin = 0, xmax = 10000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 10000, nlyrs = 5
)
xy_l <- xyFromCell(ls_terr, 1:ncell(ls_terr))
colnames(xy_l) <- c("x", "y")

elev_l <- 500 + 250 * sin(xy_l[, "x"] / 3000) -
  150 * cos(xy_l[, "y"] / 2500) + rnorm(nrow(xy_l), 0, 20)
slope_l <- pmax(1, 18 + 12 * sin((xy_l[, "x"] + xy_l[, "y"]) / 2200) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_l), 0, 2))
rain_l <- 1200 + 500 * sin(xy_l[, "x"] / 2400) + rnorm(nrow(xy_l), 0, 40)
ndvi_l <- pmin(pmax(0.6 - 0.3 * exp(-((xy_l[, "x"] - 5000)^2 +
  (xy_l[, "y"] - 5000)^2) /
  (2 * 2200^2)) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_l), 0, 0.07), 0.05), 0.9)
rock_l <- ifelse((xy_l[, "x"] / 1000 + (10000 - xy_l[, "y"]) / 1000) > 12, 1, 0)

values(ls_terr) <- cbind(elev_l, slope_l, rain_l, ndvi_l, rock_l)
names(ls_terr) <- c("elevation", "slope", "rainfall", "ndvi", "rock_soft")
```

```{r ls-maps, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.6, fig.cap="Left: continuous landslide probability. Right: engineering susceptibility zones for planning."}
ls_prob <- predict(ls_terr, ls_fit, type = "response")

qs <- quantile(values(ls_prob)[, 1], probs = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), na.rm = TRUE)
rcl_ls <- matrix(c(
  -1, qs[1], 1,
  qs[1], qs[2], 2,
  qs[2], qs[3], 3,
  qs[3], qs[4], 4,
  qs[4], 1.01, 5
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
ls_class <- classify(ls_prob, rcl_ls)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ls_prob,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "Spectral", rev = TRUE),
  main = "Landslide susceptibility (probability)"
)
plot(ls_class,
  col = c(
    "palegreen4", "palegreen3", "khaki1",
    "orange", "firebrick"
  ),
  main = "Susceptibility zones (quantile classes)"
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the pair of maps:**

- **Left:** the continuous probability map — every pixel gets a value between 0 and 1.
- **Right:** the same information collapsed into five planning zones using **quantile breaks** (each zone has ~20% of the pixels). The `classify()` function does this in one line.

Quantile zoning ensures equal-area zones. For a hazard map, you might prefer fixed thresholds (e.g., P > 0.6 = high) instead — the choice depends on whether you want equal land area per class or equal probability per class.
:::

### Area budget per zone (decision support)

```{r ls-area, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="How many hectares fall in each susceptibility class — the number the district collector asks for."}
freq_df <- as.data.frame(freq(ls_class))
cell_area_ha <- (100 * 100) / 10000 # 100 m cells -> 1 ha each
freq_df$area_ha <- freq_df$count * cell_area_ha
freq_df$zone <- c("Very low", "Low", "Moderate", "High", "Very high")[freq_df$value]

ggplot(freq_df, aes(zone, area_ha, fill = zone)) +
  geom_col(colour = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "palegreen4", "palegreen3", "khaki1",
    "orange", "firebrick"
  ), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Area by landslide susceptibility class",
    x = NULL, y = expression(Area ~ (ha))
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this bar chart:** Each bar is the **land area** (in hectares) that falls into one susceptibility class. Sum the top two bars to answer the classic policy question: *"How much of the district is high or very high risk?"* That number drives compensation budgets, relocation plans, and building restrictions. **This is the figure that goes into the executive summary of a hazard report.**
:::

## River Change Detection

**The task:** rivers migrate. Comparing channel positions between two dates quantifies **bank erosion** (land lost) and **deposition** (land gained) — critical for bridges, embankments, and land records.

::: {.civilbox}
**Civil analogy:** overlay of two survey drawings of the same river from two decades — the modern GIS does with `st_difference()` what drafters once did with tracing paper.
:::

```{r riv-polygons, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.4, fig.cap="River channel 1990 vs 2024 with eroded (red) and deposited (green) areas."}
make_channel <- function(phase = 0, amp = 900, halfw = 150, n = 300) {
  x <- seq(0, 10000, length.out = n)
  y <- 5000 + amp * sin(x / 1800 + phase)
  upper <- cbind(x, y + halfw)
  lower <- cbind(rev(x), rev(y) - halfw)
  st_polygon(list(rbind(upper, lower, upper[1, , drop = FALSE])))
}

r1990 <- st_sfc(make_channel(phase = 0, amp = 900, halfw = 150), crs = 32643)
r2024 <- st_sfc(make_channel(phase = 0.55, amp = 950, halfw = 185), crs = 32643)

erosion <- st_difference(r2024, r1990) # new channel area = bank lost
deposition <- st_difference(r1990, r2024) # abandoned channel = land gained

river_df <- st_sf(year = factor(c("1990", "2024")), geom = c(r1990, r2024))
diff_df <- st_sf(
  type = c(
    "Erosion (2024 channel over 1990 bank)",
    "Deposition (abandoned 1990 channel)"
  ),
  geom = c(erosion, deposition)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = river_df, aes(fill = year), alpha = 0.3,
    colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = diff_df, aes(fill = type), alpha = 0.85, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "1990" = "steelblue", "2024" = "darkorange",
    "Erosion (2024 channel over 1990 bank)" = "firebrick",
    "Deposition (abandoned 1990 channel)" = "forestgreen"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "River migration detection: 1990 → 2024",
    fill = NULL, x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this map:** The two channels (1990 and 2024) are overlaid. **Red areas** = land the 2024 channel occupies that the 1990 channel did not — this is bank **erosion** (land lost by landowners). **Green areas** = land the 1990 channel occupied that the 2024 channel abandoned — this is **deposition** (new land formed, often claimed by the state). Where the two overlap, the channel is stable.
:::

```{r riv-areas, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.cap="Change budget in km²: the numbers that feed compensation and design decisions."}
tibble(
  zone = c("Stable channel", "Eroded", "Deposited"),
  area_km2 = c(
    as.numeric(st_area(st_intersection(r1990, r2024))) / 1e6,
    as.numeric(st_area(erosion)) / 1e6,
    as.numeric(st_area(deposition)) / 1e6
  )
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(zone, area_km2, fill = zone)) +
  geom_col(colour = "grey25") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick", "forestgreen"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "River change budget, 1990-2024",
    x = NULL, y = expression(Area ~ (km^2))
  )
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read this chart:** Three numbers that sum to the total river-corridor area: stable (both years flooded), eroded (new flood area = land lost), deposited (abandoned flood area = land gained). **For a district administration,** erosion area × land value = compensation budget; deposition area = new revenue land. This is what makes remote sensing pay for itself.
:::

### Remote-sensing style change detection with NDVI differencing

```{r riv-ndvi-change, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="NDVI differencing between two dates: strongly negative = vegetation scoured by the flood."}
set.seed(141)
ch <- rast(
  nrows = 60, ncols = 60, xmin = 0, xmax = 6000,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 6000, nlyrs = 2
)
xy_c <- xyFromCell(ch, 1:ncell(ch))
colnames(xy_c) <- c("x", "y")

base <- pmin(pmax(0.55 + 0.1 * sin(xy_c[, "x"] / 800) +
  rnorm(nrow(xy_c), 0, 0.06), 0.05), 0.9)
d_riv <- abs(xy_c[, "y"] - (3000 + 500 * sin(xy_c[, "x"] / 1500)))
after <- base
after[d_riv < 250] <- pmax(0.08, base[d_riv < 250] - 0.35) # scour zone

values(ch) <- cbind(base, after)
names(ch) <- c("NDVI_2015", "NDVI_2024")
ndvi_diff <- ch$NDVI_2024 - ch$NDVI_2015

rcl_ch <- matrix(c(
  -1, -0.15, 2,
  -0.15, 0.15, 1,
  0.15, 1, 3
), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
chg <- classify(ndvi_diff, rcl_ch)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(ndvi_diff,
  col = hcl.colors(100, "RdYlGn"),
  main = "ΔNDVI 2024 − 2015 (red = vegetation loss)"
)
plot(chg,
  col = c("grey90", "firebrick", "forestgreen"),
  main = "Classes: grey stable, red loss, green gain"
)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.readbox}
**How to read the pair of maps:**

- **Left:** Continuous NDVI difference. Red = vegetation *lost* (scour, deforestation, urbanisation); green = vegetation *gained* (regrowth, plantations).
- **Right:** The same data classified into three zones — stable (grey), loss (red), gain (green) — using thresholds at ±0.15.

The dark-red ribbon traces the **scour zone** along the river — the same area where the channel has migrated. This is how satellite data tells you *where the river has eaten the bank*, without ever visiting the site.
:::

# One-Page Summary (Pin This!)

| Concept | One-line takeaway |
|---|---|
| Linear regression | Fits a line by least squares — interpret slope as physical sensitivity |
| Logistic regression | Sigmoid of a linear score gives P(event); odds ratios for interpretation |
| Decision tree | Yes/no flowchart learned from data; overfits without pruning |
| Random forest | Committee of decorrelated trees; OOB error is a free test estimate |
| Variable importance | Which features the forest relies on most; guides factor-map design |
| Partial dependence | Shape of one feature's effect holding others constant |
| KNN | Majority vote of nearest neighbours; always scale features; tune k |
| Naive Bayes | Bayes' theorem + independent-features assumption; fast, transparent |
| K-means | Partition into K clusters by centroid distance; elbow + silhouette pick K |
| Hierarchical | Agglomerative tree of merges; dendrogram cut at height gives K |
| Raster | Grid of cells — DEMs, imagery, rainfall surfaces (`terra`) |
| Vector | Points, lines, polygons — pipes, parcels, rivers (`sf`) |
| NDVI | (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red); vegetation health proxy |
| GIS + AI fusion | `extract()` map→table, train, `predict()` table→map |
| UHI | City centre runs hotter; quantify with LST and NDVI regression |
| Landslide susceptibility | Logistic/forest model of slope, rain, NDVI, rock → probability map |
| River change | Overlay two dates; erosion vs deposition areas in km² |

---

# Mini Glossary

- **Feature / predictor** — an input column the model learns from (age, rainfall, NDVI).
- **Label / target** — what we predict (strength, flood yes/no, condition class).
- **Sigmoid** — the S-curve $1/(1+e^{-z})$ that squashes a linear score into [0, 1].
- **Odds ratio** — $e^{\beta}$; multiplicative change in odds per unit increase in a predictor.
- **Gini impurity / entropy** — purity measures used to choose tree splits.
- **Bootstrap sample** — random rows with replacement; the base ingredient of bagging.
- **Bagging** — bootstrap aggregating; trains trees on resampled rows to decorrelate them.
- **OOB (out-of-bag)** — the ~37% of rows each tree never saw; the forest's free validation set.
- **Variable importance** — a score of how much each feature contributes to forest accuracy.
- **Partial dependence** — average model prediction as one feature sweeps its range.
- **Linkage** — the rule defining distance between clusters (single, complete, average, Ward).
- **Dendrogram** — tree diagram of hierarchical merges.
- **Silhouette width** — per-point clustering quality in [−1, 1]; near 1 = well placed.
- **Raster / vector** — cell-grid vs. coordinate-geometry spatial data models.
- **CRS** — coordinate reference system; defines what the numbers on the map mean.
- **NDVI** — normalized difference vegetation index;
